summary: Defines a DHCP option and a Router Advertisement extension to tell clients they are behind a captive portal and must authenticate for Internet access, as in coffee shops. It was replaced by RFC 8910.

eli5.summary: At a cafe your device is told 'sign in first'. It was replaced by RFC 8910.

questions: how does a device detect a captive portal
what is the dhcp captive portal option
how does captive portal option work
subtitle: Tells devices they are behind a captive portal that requires authentication.

tldr.problem: When devices connect to networks in places like coffee shops, they do not automatically know they are behind a captive portal and cannot access the Internet until they authenticate.
tldr.mechanism: A DHCP option (for IPv4) and Router Advertisement extension (for IPv6) can inform clients of the captive portal's URI, so the system knows to display an authentication page rather than relying on interception techniques.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8910 replaced this with a more complete method, but this specification provided a standard way for networks to advertise captive portals without resorting to man-in-the-middle tricks.

today: RFC 7710 is an Internet Standard as originally published. It has been obsoleted by RFC 8910, which provides additional methods for captive portal detection and a more complete specification.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Users in temporary network environments like coffee shops must often authenticate through a captive portal before accessing the Internet. The RFC defines a standard method for networks to announce the presence of a captive portal to connecting clients.

Traditionally, captive portal devices have used interception techniques similar to man-in-the-middle attacks to force clients to authenticate. This document specifies DHCP options for IPv4 and Router Advertisement (RA) extensions for IPv6 that allow networks to inform clients of the captive portal's location directly, rather than relying on interception.
sections.eli5: Networks can now tell your device 'there is a login page here' using official messages, instead of secretly intercepting your web traffic.

sections.title: The Captive-Portal Option
sections.content:
The RFC defines three versions of the captive-portal option.

IPv4 DHCP Option (160): Contains a one-byte code and length field, followed by a URI (up to 255 bytes) pointing to the authentication page. The URI SHOULD be an IP address literal to avoid requiring DNS interception.

IPv6 DHCP Option (103): Uses a similar structure with a 16-bit option code and 16-bit length field, followed by the URI in variable length.

IPv6 Router Advertisement Option (Type 37): Embedded in Router Advertisement messages, this option includes a Type field, Length field (in 8-byte units), and the URI padded with NULL bytes to align to 8-byte boundaries.

All three versions carry the same essential information: a URI that tells the client where to authenticate. Operators should use the same URI across all three methods to reduce operational problems.
sections.eli5: The network sends a message with a special label (option 160 for IPv4, 103 for IPv6, or type 37 in router ads) that contains the URL of the login page.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: The IANA has assigned option code 160 from the BOOTP Vendor Extensions and DHCP Options registry for IPv4 DHCP, option code 103 from the DHCPv6 Option Codes registry for IPv6 DHCP, and option type 37 from the IPv6 Neighbor Discovery Option Formats registry (ICMPv6 parameters) for the RA extension.
sections.eli5: Official registry numbers were assigned to make sure networks and devices all use the same labels for the captive portal message.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
An attacker able to inject DHCP or RA messages could direct users to a malicious login page. However, an attacker with this capability could already intercept all traffic by listing themselves as the default gateway. This option removes the need for interception, allowing operating systems and applications to render the authentication page in a sandboxed environment and clearly label it as untrusted.

By providing a legitimate way to announce captive portals, this method improves security by eliminating the need for users to disable security features like DNSSEC validation or VPNs to access the network. The system can treat captive portal connections differently from normal traffic and avoid sending sensitive credentials or cookies to the portal until fully authenticated.

TLS can protect the captive portal URI to help reassure users they are connecting to the intended portal.
sections.eli5: Bad actors could trick you with a fake login page, but you should only see this message from your local network, and you can be extra careful with security while signing in.
